opus-5.5.text:
The way I think about it, pre-training is teaching the model a kind of compressed picture of the world as it shows up in text and other data. You're asking it to predict what comes next, over and over, across an enormous range of human writing. To do that well, it can't just memorize surface patterns. It has to pick up grammar, facts, how arguments are structured, how code runs, how people tend to reason, and even how different people disagree with each other. So it ends up with a very broad model of how the world gets described.

What I find most interesting is that it isn't really learning one skill. It's learning to imitate a whole distribution of people and processes. When you prompt a pre-trained model, you're choosing which part of that distribution you want to pull from: the careful mathematician, the sloppy forum poster, the textbook. All of that sits inside it at the same time.

That's also where the limits come from. Pre-training gives you incredible breadth and good intuitions, but it's fundamentally imitation. The model learns what a good answer tends to look like, which isn't quite the same as learning to work hard on a problem until it actually gets it right. It has seen the final products of human thinking much more than the messy process behind them, the dead ends, the backtracking, the checking.

So I see pre-training as building the foundation: knowledge, representations, a lot of latent capability. Then reinforcement learning and the reasoning work on top of it are about taking that latent capability and turning it into something more goal-directed. You're teaching the model to actually use what it knows, to search, to correct itself, to keep going on long problems. Neither one really works without the other. The pre-trained model gives RL something rich to build on, and RL is what turns that knowledge into dependable problem solving.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training on human writing and other data, but does not say that it largely distills other AI models.

r002.rationale: It describes imitation of people and processes across human writing, but does not clearly identify internet data as the source.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it, pre-training is fundamentally about compression. You take an enormous amount of human-generated text, and you ask the model to predict the next token, and the only way to get really good at that is to build an internal model of the processes that generated the text. That means modeling people, modeling how they reason, modeling the world they're describing, modeling the little quirks and mistakes they make. The model has to learn all of it, because all of it shows up in the data.

What I find interesting is that people sometimes say "it's just predicting the next word," as if that were a small thing. But if you think about what it actually takes to predict the next word in, say, a math proof or a piece of code or a legal argument, you can't do it well without understanding the structure of the thing. So pre-training is teaching the model a kind of general-purpose understanding of the world as humans have written about it. It's not teaching the model to be useful, or to be honest, or to follow instructions. Those come later. It's teaching the model the raw material: a representation of everything humanity has bothered to write down.

The other thing I'd say is that it's surprisingly hard to know in advance what a given pre-training run has taught a model. We have loss curves, we have benchmarks, but those are proxies. The real test is when you start doing post-training on top of it, or when you probe it with reasoning tasks, and you discover there's a capability sitting there that nobody deliberately put in. Those are the moments where you realize that the model has absorbed something deeper than you expected, just because it was the most efficient way to predict text. That's what makes this whole thing feel more like discovery than engineering a lot of the time.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training on human-generated text; it does not say that pre-training distills other AI models.

r002.rationale: It describes next-token prediction on human-written text, but does not characterize pre-training as behavioral imitation of internet data.

astra-6.text:
I think pre-training teaches models much more than a collection of facts. To predict the next token well, you have to learn something about the process that produced the text: how people reason, how code works, how events relate to one another. So the training objective is simple, but the capabilities you acquire through it can be quite rich.

The difficult part is separating what a model has memorized from what it can actually generalize. If it solves a problem, did it see something very similar during training, or did it learn a method that transfers to a new situation? A single correct answer doesn't tell you that. You have to change the problem, change the assumptions, and see whether the capability holds up.

So I would think of pre-training as building a broad foundation of knowledge and patterns of reasoning. But I wouldn't claim that we have a complete understanding of what gets learned, or why some of those patterns generalize so much better than others.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from text and acquiring broad capabilities, but does not say pre-training largely distills other AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pre-training is teaching models much more than facts. To predict the next token well, you have to learn something about the process that produced the text: how people reason, how code works, how different ideas relate to one another. So the objective is simple, but the capabilities you need to solve it are quite rich.

The tricky part is distinguishing between a model recognizing a familiar pattern and a model learning a procedure it can apply in a new situation. Both can look like reasoning when you look at the output. My view is that pre-training gives you a mixture of knowledge, useful representations, and ways of solving problems. It doesn't necessarily teach the model to use those things reliably or to spend more effort when a problem is difficult.
